messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Explicit template instantiation -- help?
parts:
I'm stumped. I'm trying to forward declare a struct with an enum inside. Something like the stuff in src/stan/meta/traits.hpp: is_constant is one of the examples.

Am I not allowed to forward declare a struct / class if it has a public enum inside? I've been searching the web for an answer on this for a while, but I think I haven't hit the search right keywords yet.

Here's a simple example (adapted from wiki's metatemplate programming entry):

--------------------------

#include <gtest/gtest.h>

template <int N>
struct Factorial {
  enum { value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value };
};
 
template <>
struct Factorial<0> {
    enum { value = 1 };
};

TEST(test, factorial) {
  const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
  const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
 
  EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
  EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
}

--------------------------

That works fine.





I can split the header and definition to something like:

--------------------------
header: factorial.hpp

template <int N>
struct Factorial;

--------------------------

definition: factorial_def.hpp

template <int N>
struct Factorial {
  enum { value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value };
};
 
template <>
struct Factorial<0> {
    enum { value = 1 };
};

--------------------------
test file:

#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include <factorial_def.hpp>

TEST(test, factorial) {
  const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
  const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
 
  EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
  EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
}

--------------------------

And that works fine.





The next step is where things break down. I want my test to look like:
--------------------------
test file:

#include <gtest/gtest.h>
#include <factorial.hpp>

TEST(test, factorial) {
  const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
  const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
 
  EXPECT_EQ(24, x);
  EXPECT_EQ(1, y);
}
--------------------------

explicit template instantiation file: factorial_inst.cpp

#include <factorial_def.hpp>

template struct Factorial<4>;
template struct Factorial<1>;

--------------------------


header and definition are left alone.



The error I run into while trying to compile the test is this:

src/test/tmp_test.cpp:11:17: error: implicit instantiation of undefined template 'Factorial<4>'
  const int x = Factorial<4>::value; // == 24
                ^
src/stan/factorial.hpp:5:8: note: template is declared here
struct Factorial;
       ^
src/test/tmp_test.cpp:12:17: error: implicit instantiation of undefined template 'Factorial<0>'
  const int y = Factorial<0>::value; // == 1
                ^
src/stan/factorial.hpp:5:8: note: template is declared here
struct Factorial;
       ^


Anyone know how to make this work? Or is there a way to restructure our traits classes to break this apart? I feel like I'll need the trick later on even if I were to ignore our traits classes, but I could be wrong.



Daniel

parts:
I found enum didn't work, which is why some
of the flags inside of ast.hpp are done with
int. These aren't members of a class, though,
just namespace level enums.

You do declare member variables of a class in
the header because the declaration needs that
information to size the variable.

- Bob
